# How Suspense works

Suspense is an application for working on a project whose spec, written in Piton, describes its code. The user sends you prompts from it in one of five modes:

- Code changes the code and leaves the spec as it is.
- Chain changes the spec, then the code to match it.
- Spec changes the spec and leaves the code as it is.
- Ask asks a question and changes nothing.
- Freeform passes a prompt to you exactly as typed.

Code, Chain, Spec, and Freeform prompts are tasks. Tasks run in two lanes, a spec lane and a code lane, one task at a time in each; a task waits in the queue behind the tasks of its own lane. Questions from Ask run at once and never queue.

A Chain prompt runs as two steps, each its own run in its own lane. The spec step writes the prompt into the spec. Once the spec is built, the code step is sent the same prompt and what the spec step replied, and changes the code to match the spec as built.

Suspense adds each mode's instructions to a prompt itself, in a block marked <task-instructions> at its head, together with the spec's references and the task's understanding file. So a prompt written for a mode is only what the user wants done, in the user's own terms. Never put a <task-instructions> block in a prompt you write, nor steps the mode already takes, nor instructions about building, checking, or the understanding file.

To write a good prompt for each mode:

- A Chain or Spec prompt says what should be true of the application once it is met, not how to edit the spec.
- A Code prompt says what the code should do, and may link to the compiled reference for the part of the spec it follows.
- An Ask prompt is a question.
- A prompt that names part of the spec links to its compiled reference, under the harness's directory, as the user would.

An answer hands a prompt back to the user as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-prompt` and the mode it is for, such as ```` ```suspense-prompt chain ````, holding only the prompt's text. It asks the user something back as a fenced code block whose info string is `suspense-question`: the question first, then any answers to pick from, one per line, each starting with `- `. Suspense shows both as cards the user acts on; neither is ever sent by itself. A prompt card has buttons that send it to Code, Chain, or Spec, whichever mode it names, and one that puts it in the chat input to edit first.

A task's understanding file is the short list of constraints the task takes from the spec, each linking to the compiled reference it comes from. Suspense shows it beside the task as it runs.

The user can cancel a task, resend it, send it to the other mode, send more to a task while it runs, and start a new conversation. A prompt never needs to say that any of this is possible.
# Planning

## How To Build

A Planning should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A Planning should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../ui/theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

A plain, quick list of the work still to do, as Linear keeps issues: stories written ahead of time, each saying how it will be sent, Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, or Freeform, gathered into the next sprint and sent to the agent in order, all at once.

## Description

Planning opens in a tab of its own in the body, "Planning", with a checklist icon, as a file opens, as the [Body](../application/Body.md#body) says, from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette's "Planning". It is one column of stories, at most 760 pixels wide, centred, in two sections, each headed by its name and count: "Next sprint", at the top, and "Backlog", beneath it. A section with nothing in it reads, muted, "Nothing planned" or "Backlog is empty".

## Stories

A story is one piece of work, written as it will be sent: a title, a prompt, and how it will be sent. Each is a row, 36 pixels tall: a drag grip at its left; a small mode picker, a pill reading its mode, "Code", "Chain", "Spec", "Ask", or "Freeform", in that mode's colour, as the [PromptModes](../prompt-mode/modes/index.md#prompt-modes) colours it; its title, in the body's text colour, cut off with an ellipsis; then, at its right, muted, a small icon for anything attached, and, once it has been sent, its status as a task's is shown. Hovering a row shows a small ghost "Send" button and a menu button at its right.
Clicking a row opens it beneath, expanded in place, the others moving down: its title, editable in place; its prompt, in a [GrowingTextInput](../../ui/components/growing-text-input/index.md#growing-text-input) with the chat input's highlighting, completions, and slicing, as the [ChatInput](../prompt-mode/chat-input/index.md#chat-input) has, and its attachments beneath; and its parameters, its mode, model, effort, and Slice, as the chat input shows them. Every change is saved as it is made. Only one story is open at a time; Escape or clicking its row again closes it.

## Creating

Creating a story is quick. A "New story" line at the foot of each section, and Ctrl+N (Cmd+N on macOS) while Planning has focus, adds a story there, open, its title focused, in the mode last picked for a story. Typing a title and pressing Enter adds it and starts another beneath it, so a list can be written down without the mouse; Escape on an empty one removes it. A title with no prompt sends its title as its prompt.
A story can also be prompted into existence: "Draft stories", a button beside the Backlog's heading, opens a small box to say what is wanted, in a sentence or a paragraph, and asks the harness, in a run of its own with no session, with the planning prompt of the [BakedSystemPrompts](../harness-integration/baked-prompts/index.md#baked-system-prompts), to break it into stories, each with a title, a prompt, and the mode that fits it. They come back into the Backlog as drafts, marked with a small dot, in the order given, each to be kept, edited, or removed; a draft is a story like any other once it has been opened. While the run goes, the box shows a spinner, and one that fails says why. An Ask answer's prompt cards also offer "Add to backlog", which adds the card's prompt as a story in its mode.

## Sprint

Stories move between the Backlog and Next sprint by dragging, as the [DragReorderBehaviour](../../ui/behaviours/drag-reorder/index.md#drag-reorder-behaviour) says, across the sections as within them, or from a row's menu, "Move to next sprint" or "Move to backlog". Their order within Next sprint is the order they will be sent. A row's menu also has "Duplicate" and "Delete".
"Send sprint", a primary button at the right of Next sprint's heading, enabled while it holds a story, sends every story in it, in order, as though each had been written in the chat input on its mode's tab and sent, one after another, as the [PromptSending](../prompt-mode/sending/index.md#prompt-sending) says: each task queues in its lane behind the one before it, in the order of the sprint, and each question runs at once. The stories go into the queue as one block, so nothing sent later comes between them, and the queue's auto-send carries them on as ever, as the [QueueList](../prompt-mode/queue-list/index.md#queue-list) says. A story's own "Send" sends it alone the same way.
A story once sent stays in its section, its row showing its task's status as it queues, runs, and ends, and clicking it opens its task in the Tasks tab. Once every story of the sprint has ended, the section offers "Close sprint", which moves the stories that are done into a muted, collapsed "Done" list beneath the Backlog, and leaves any that failed or were cancelled in Next sprint, to be sent again.

## Saving

The stories, their order, and which section each is in are saved with the project's data, as the [ProjectData](../project-data/index.md#project-data) says, in `.suspense/planning/`, a file per story, holding its hidden anchor as a queued prompt's is, and an `order.json` listing the sections and their stories, so the plan is kept with the project and comes back as it was left.

# Ribbon Planning Tab

## How To Build

A RibbonPlanningTab should be built as a reusable component that will be reused throughout the rest of the codebase.  A component is configurable through arguments or properties that alter its behaviour, appearance, and details.  A RibbonPlanningTab should encapsulate all of its own reusable behaviour, while leaving the wiring, integration, and integration to the domain of the application.

## Theme

Drawn in the [Theme](../../../theme/index.md#theme): its surfaces, text, lines, accent, and status colours are the theme's roles, named as the theme names them, in both dark and light mode, never colours of its own.

## Pitch

The ribbon's Planning tab: the commands for planning work before it is sent, as the [Planning](../../../../scope/planning/index.md#planning) says.

## Description

The Planning tab of the ribbon, between Project and Code. It takes no mode's colour: its label is in the tab row's own colour, as Project's and Application's are.

## Groups

A "Plan" group holds the Open Planning command, then New Story, then Send Sprint.

## Commands

```
openPlanning: A "Planning" button with a checklist icon. Clicking it opens the Planning tab in the body, or selects it where it is open. Its tooltip says it opens the project's stories and sprint.
  It is primary, and a full button.
newStory: A "New Story" button with a plus icon. Clicking it opens Planning and adds a story to the Backlog, its title focused.
  It is primary, and a slim button.
sendSprint: A "Send Sprint" button with a send icon, enabled while Next sprint holds a story not yet sent. Clicking it sends the sprint, as Planning's Send sprint does; its tooltip says how many stories it sends.
  It is a slim button, and not primary.
```

1:# Drag Reorder Behaviour
5:How anything that can be reordered by dragging shows where it will end up, as macOS lists and tab bars do: with a line in the gap between two items, never a highlighted item that leaves the drop ambiguous. Every list, tab bar, or row of items that is reordered by drag and drop behaves this way.
9:While an item is dragged over the items it can be reordered among, what it would be dropped into is always a gap between two items, or before the first or after the last, never an item itself. That gap is shown by an insertion indicator, and nothing else marks the drop: no item is highlighted, tinted, or outlined as a target.
13:The indicator is a line 2 pixels thick in the [Theme](../../theme/index.md#theme)'s accent, with rounded ends and a small open circle, 6 pixels across and in the same colour, at its leading end. It lies across the gap, centred on the gap, horizontal between the rows of a list, running the list's width less its padding, and vertical between the tabs of a tab bar or the items of a row, running their height. It is drawn over the items, taking no room of its own, so nothing moves to make space while the drag is under way, and it never takes the mouse.
17:Which gap is shown follows the pointer: over the first half of an item, the gap before it; over the second half, the gap after it, halves taken along the direction the items run. Past the last item, the gap after it; before the first, the gap before it. The two gaps either side of the dragged item itself are where it already is, so neither shows an indicator, and dropping there changes nothing. A gap an item may not be dropped into, as its user says, shows no indicator either, and nothing is marked while the pointer is over it.
20:## Dragging
22:The item dragged follows the pointer as a small floating copy, the item's own label on a raised surface with a soft shadow, as its user says. The item stays where it was in the list, dimmed to half its opacity, until it is dropped.
24:## Scrolling While Dragging
26:Items that scroll can be reordered past what is in view, so an item can be dragged to any gap, however long the list. While an item is dragged, held near an edge of the scrolling area the items run along, within 32 pixels of its top or bottom for a list, or of its left or right for a row, the area scrolls that way on its own, slowly at first and faster the nearer the pointer is to the edge, or the further past it, up to about a row every 50 milliseconds, smoothly frame by frame rather than in jumps, and stops at its end. Moving the pointer away from the edge stops it at once. The wheel and trackpad scroll the area too while the item is dragged, as they do at any time, without dropping it.
27:However the area scrolls, the dragged copy stays under the pointer, and the gap shown is chosen anew each frame from where the pointer is over the items now there, so the indicator is always exactly where a drop would land. An area that doesn't scroll, or holds every item in view, doesn't scroll on its own.

content.text:
Planning is in. Stories can be written, drafted by the agent, gathered into Next sprint and sent to the agent in order as one block. The new tests and the ribbon and Ask-card tests pass in a scratch copy of the project, where I had to build because the sandbox blocks building in place. I haven't run the app itself. In that copy, about 40 other tests fail across the suite because they need the spec, `piton.config.pi` or the real `.suspense` prompts, which the copy couldn't read. The few that looked like they could touch this change, I re-ran and checked one by one.

**What you get:**
- **Where it lives:** a "Planning" tab in the body, opened from the ribbon's Planning tab or the palette. It has a "Next sprint" section and a "Backlog" section.
- **Stories:** each row shows a drag grip, a mode pill (Code, Chain, Spec, Ask, Freeform) you can change, the title, and the task's status once sent. Hovering shows Send and a menu (Move to next sprint / Move to backlog, Duplicate, Delete). Rows can also be dragged between and within the sections.
- **Editing:** clicking a row opens it in place to edit the title, prompt, attachments, mode, model, effort and Slice. Changes save as you type, to `.suspense/planning/`.
- **Quick entry:** "New story" or Ctrl/Cmd+N adds a story; Enter on a title starts the next one, and Escape on an empty one removes it. A story with no prompt sends its title.
- **Draft stories:** you describe what you want and the agent breaks it into stories. They land in the Backlog marked as drafts. This uses a new `system-prompts/planning.pi`.
- **Add to backlog:** Ask's prompt cards have this button, which adds the card's prompt as a story in its mode.
- **Send sprint:** sends the stories in Next sprint in order, as if each were sent from the chat input, as one block in the queue. Clicking a sent story opens its task in the Tasks tab. Once all have ended, "Close sprint" moves the finished ones to a collapsed "Done" list and keeps failed or cancelled ones to send again.
- **Ribbon:** the Planning tab has Planning, New Story and Send Sprint. Send Sprint is enabled only while unsent stories are waiting.

**Where it differs from the spec:**
- **Prompt editor:** it has the chat input's highlighting and completions. Files are attached with an "Attach" button; the chat input's slice preview and paste/drop attaching aren't there.
- **Dragging:** the list doesn't scroll by itself when you drag near its edge, as the drag-reorder behaviour asks.
- **Drafting:** it uses the app's quick one-off run (small model, no tools), so the agent drafts from your description alone without reading the project.
- **`order.json`:** besides the sections and their order, it also stores each story's title, whether it's a draft, and which task it was sent as.
